meta.title: Who really said "All wars are planned by older men in council rooms apart"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Grantland Rice wrote it — in his poem “The Two Sides of War,” New York Tribune, 26 March 1921. The familiar “old men” version is a 1955 Bartlett’s alteration.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All wars are planned by older men in council rooms apart'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Grantland Rice, “The Two Sides of War,” New York Tribune, 26 March 1921 — and Rice wrote “older men,” not the familiar “old men.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The line opens Rice’s poem “The Two Sides of War,” published in his syndicated column “The Sportlight” in the New York Tribune on 26 March 1921. Quote Investigator published and transcribed that printing — located by researcher Jonathan Lighter — which reads “All wars are planned by older men / In council rooms apart” — the familiar “old men” wording is a later alteration.

source.heading: The 1921 printing

docMeta.dd: “The Sportlight,” New York Tribune, 26 March 1921, p. 11, col. 2
Quote Investigator, 2 February 2020 (citation located by Jonathan Lighter)

source.excerpt:
All wars are planned by older men
In council rooms apart,
Who plan for greater armament
And map the battle chart.

… But where their sightless eyes stare out
Beyond life’s vanished joys,
I’ve noticed nearly all the dead
Were hardly more than boys.
trail: 1866 — Herman Melville publishes Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War, whose “The March into Virginia” contains, as its sixth line, “All wars are boyish, and are fought by boys” ↗ — the same thought, well before Rice.
26 March 1921 — Grantland Rice prints “The Two Sides of War” in his column “The Sportlight” in the New York Tribune, p. 11, col. 2: the earliest printing documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

28 June 1944 — Herbert Hoover, addressing the Republican national convention, says “Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die” — a separate remark on the same theme, reported in the Chicago Tribune, 28 June 1944, p. 5 ↗.

1955 — the 13th edition of Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations prints Rice’s first stanza as “All wars are planned by old men” — the earliest appearance of the shortened form Quote Investigator records ↗; the 1989 Macmillan Dictionary of Quotations carries it too.
source.excerptNote: Wording follows the 1921 New York Tribune text as transcribed by Quote Investigator. Widely circulated online copies differ in several words — see below.

author.name: Grantland Rice
author.heading: About Grantland Rice
author.bio: Henry Grantland Rice was the most widely read American sportswriter of the early twentieth century, syndicated for decades under the column title “The Sportlight” and best remembered for christening Notre Dame’s “Four Horsemen.” He was also a working versifier: his columns carried original poems, and he published books of verse. “The Two Sides of War” is the Rice poem that circulates most widely outside the sports pages — a short, plain-spoken piece about who votes for war and who dies in it.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and what actually changed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Rice is sound; the wording and the speaker are what go wrong in circulation.

items.why: Rice wrote “older men.” The 13th edition of Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations (1955) printed “old men,” and later reference works — including the Macmillan Dictionary of Quotations (1989) — carried the shortened form forward, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Hoover’s 1944 remark — “Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die” — is a separate statement on the same theme, quoted in the Chicago Tribune and documented alongside Rice’s poem by Quote Investigator ↗. It is not the source of Rice’s verse.

The sixth line of “The March into Virginia,” in Melville’s Battle-Pieces (1866), reads “All wars are boyish, and are fought by boys” ↗ — the same sentiment, different lines. Quote Investigator lists it as an antecedent, not as the origin of Rice’s stanza.

Copies circulating online read “Who call for greater armament,” “martial note” and “vanished toys.” The 1921 newspaper printing transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ reads “Who plan for greater armament.” Quote Investigator does note that Rice’s own 1955 collection The Final Answer and Other Poems reprints the poem with the first verse identical to 1921 and the later verses revised slightly — which may account for the later-stanza readings. The first-stanza reading “call for greater armament” is documented in neither printing.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Grantland Rice’s, first printed in his column in the New York Tribune on 26 March 1921 — and he wrote “older men,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Rice was writing in 1921, with the Great War close behind him and arguments over “greater armament” still live. The poem is four short stanzas of exactly one idea, stated twice: elders vote, boys die.

Its afterlife is bigger than its author. The verse escaped the sports page, entered quotation dictionaries, and now circulates mostly as a stand-alone epigram — usually in the smoothed “old men” form and often with no name attached at all. Herbert Hoover’s separate 1944 remark on the same theme travels in the same company.
detailsBody: Two things happened to the text. First, quotation books trimmed it: the earliest printing of the shortened “old men” form that Quote Investigator records is the 13th edition of Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations (1955), and the 1989 Macmillan Dictionary of Quotations carries it too. Quote Investigator does not establish where the change originated.

Second, the poem now travels through poetry aggregator sites in a version that differs from the 1921 printing at several points (“call for greater armament,” “martial note,” “vanished toys”). There is one documented lead: Quote Investigator notes that Rice’s own 1955 collection The Final Answer and Other Poems reprints the poem with the first verse identical to 1921 but the later verses revised slightly, which may account for the later-stanza variants. The first-stanza reading “call for greater armament” is documented in neither printing, so treat the 1921 newspaper text as the reference.
